title: General versus monotone span programs
formal:
Do there exist nonconstant monotone Boolean functions \(f_n:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}\) with polynomial-size general span programs over \(\mathbb F_2\), but no polynomial-size monotone span programs over that same field? The exact separation asks for one family satisfying
\[\exists C,d\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1,\quad\mathrm{SP}_{\mathbb F_2}(f_n)\le C(n+1)^d,\]
\[\forall C',d'\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n_0\ge1\ \exists n\ge n_0,\quad\mathrm{mSP}_{\mathbb F_2}(f_n)>C'(n+1)^{d'}.\]
Yes: the STOC 2018 all-field lower bounds for directed layered connectivity, together with its polynomial-size general span programs over \(\mathbb F_2\), give the required same-field separation. The historical question is resolved and archived.
why: The affirmative separation proves that allowing negative input tests can greatly reduce the size of a span program even when the final function is monotone. It resolves a basic limitation of monotone linear-algebraic computation.
status_note: Resolved affirmatively by Pitassi–Robere, STOC 2018, DOI 10.1145/3188745.3188914. The published introduction explicitly combines polynomial-size nonmonotone span programs for directed connectivity over GF(2) with the paper’s superpolynomial monotone lower bounds over all fields; §7/Theorem 7.1 and full ECCC Appendix B/Theorem B.1 provide the layered-connectivity application. The original source fixes GF(2), and both bounds therefore concern the same field. The nonuniform upper-bound provenance was checked against Wigderson’s author record and visually readable first page; no uniform simulation or class equality is inferred. The lower-bound application and full-version rank-lifting proof were read, but this review is not a complete independent proof audit or a Lean formalization.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 2026-09-16; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

sentences: The historical target asks whether a monotone function can have short general span programs but only large monotone span programs over GF(2).
General programs may enable rows using either positive or negative literals, whereas monotone programs use only positive literals.
Size is the number of rows and the families are nonuniform.
The STOC 2018 directed-connectivity lower bound, combined with the known polynomial general-program upper bound, gives the requested same-field separation.
The card is resolved and archived with the precise theorem and model recorded.

definitions:
A Boolean function is monotone when \(x_i\le y_i\) for every coordinate implies \(f(x)\le f(y)\). Nonconstant monotone functions satisfy \(f(0^n)=0\) and \(f(1^n)=1\); the known separating examples have this property, so no constant-function convention is involved. Monotonicity is a property of the function’s truth table. It does not by itself require the program computing it to avoid negated tests.

Fix \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\), with arithmetic modulo 2. A general span program on \(n\) input bits consists of a finite matrix \(M\in\mathbb F_2^{s\times t}\), a fixed nonzero target \(w\in\mathbb F_2^t\), and one literal label on each row. A literal is either \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\); labels may repeat. On input \(x\), retain a row labeled \(x_i\) when \(x_i=1\), and retain a row labeled \(\neg x_i\) when \(x_i=0\). Accept if and only if \(w\) is a linear combination over \(\mathbb F_2\) of the retained rows. The empty set of rows spans only the zero vector. The program computes \(f\) if its answer equals \(f(x)\) for every input.

A monotone span program has exactly the same acceptance condition, but permits only positive row labels \(x_i\). Its linear algebra may still use cancellation modulo 2. Size is the number \(s\) of rows, not matrix bit length, number of columns or the time needed to test span membership. Let \(\mathrm{SP}_{\mathbb F_2}(f)\) and \(\mathrm{mSP}_{\mathbb F_2}(f)\) be the minimum row counts for the general and monotone models respectively. Any finite column dimension and any fixed nonzero target are allowed; changing coordinates gives the source’s equivalent all-ones target convention. There are no sparsity or unique-label restrictions. Redundant dimensions may be removed because the rows and target span a space of dimension at most \(s+1\).

This is an exact, nonuniform size comparison. Each length may have its own finite matrix, labels and target, with no requirement that a single efficient algorithm generate them. The upper-bound polynomial must nevertheless have constants independent of the input length. The program has no random coins, approximation error or advice depending on the particular input assignment. The lower bound ranges over every permitted monotone matrix representation at that length.

The two models use the same fixed field \(\mathbb F_2\), as stipulated at the start of the source chapter. Comparing a small program over one field to large monotone programs over another field would not by itself answer this card. The later theorem proves monotone lower bounds over every field; the general-program upper bound over \(\mathbb F_2\) is sufficient for the required comparison. The second displayed condition means that no fixed polynomial bounds all minimum monotone sizes and that violations occur at arbitrarily large lengths. Graph-family parameters in the resolution have polynomially related edge-input lengths, so their quasipolynomial bounds remain superpolynomial in the number of actual input bits.
answer_criterion: The original target requires a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existence statement. A positive answer must define one monotone family, prove its polynomial general-program upper bound and prove its superpolynomial monotone-program lower bound over the same \(\mathbb F_2\) model. A refutation would exclude every such family. A constant-factor gap, different-field comparison, restricted lower-bound model or conditional separation would not suffice. The asymptotic quantifiers are exact. The published affirmative separation retires this question from the open benchmark; recording that resolution does not claim that its complete proof has already been formalized in Lean.

source_formulation.text: Research Problem 8.12 asks for a monotone function family with polynomial-size ordinary span programs and superpolynomial monotone span-program size.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Research Problem 8.12, retaining the chapter’s GF(2) convention and nonuniform size measure

context_blocks.text: A monotone function never changes from true to false when more input bits become 1. Nevertheless, a program computing it may use negative tests internally. The historical question asks whether forbidding those tests can force a superpolynomial increase in a linear-algebraic representation.

The source compares this issue with known gaps between monotone and general Boolean circuits. Such circuit gaps cannot simply be transferred to span programs, because the latter compute through linear dependence and may exploit cancellation even when their row labels are positive.

The 2018 paper identifies directed layered connectivity as a separating function: general span programs over \(\mathbb F_2\) have polynomial size, whereas monotone span programs over every field require quasipolynomial size. In terms of the edge-input length \(N\), the latter lower bound is \(N^{\Omega(\log N)}\), which exceeds every fixed polynomial.

The input to layered connectivity specifies which edges exist between consecutive layers of a fixed directed graph. The function asks whether there is a source-to-target path. It is total and monotone in the edge bits. The source’s existential question does not require an arbitrary monotone function to have such a gap.

The known general-program upper bound is nonuniform, consistent with the card’s model. Wigderson’s earlier work provides a nonuniform containment of nondeterministic logarithmic-space computation in parity logarithmic-space computation, used by the span-program literature to obtain this upper bound. No uniform deterministic logarithmic-space reachability algorithm follows from the size statement.

The result shows that a monotone specification can benefit essentially from negative tests inside a span program. Through the connection to linear secret sharing, monotone size also measures the difficulty of representing monotone authorization rules by linear shares; the general program is a different representation model.
